title: Arbitration and Conciliation Act s. 10 — Statutory provision (ACA s. 10)

content.overview: Section 10 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 governs the number of arbitrators. Parties may determine the number, but the number cannot be even. If they fail to determine the number, the statutory default is a sole arbitrator.
content.glance: Section 10 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 governs the number of arbitrators. Parties may determine the number, but the number cannot be even. If they fail to determine the number, the statutory default is a sole arbitrator.
content.study:
Section 10 — Number of arbitrators

Section 10(1) preserves party autonomy on the constitution of the arbitral tribunal, subject to one express statutory limit: the number of arbitrators determined by the parties shall not be an even number.

Section 10(2) supplies the default where the parties have not determined the number of arbitrators: the arbitral tribunal shall consist of a sole arbitrator.

The section must be read with the provisions governing appointment and composition of the tribunal. It is not itself the appointment mechanism. Its immediate function is to determine the permissible number of arbitrators and the statutory default.

The statutory rule creates two basic enquiries:
1. Did the parties determine the number of arbitrators?
2. If so, is that number permissible because it is not even? If the parties did not determine the number, the tribunal consists of one arbitrator by operation of section 10(2).

The provision is concise, but its drafting consequence is important: an arbitration clause should be read for its actual agreement on tribunal size rather than replacing the parties' chosen number with a generic assumption about a three-member tribunal.

sections.heading: 1. Party autonomy subject to an odd-number requirement
sections.body: Section 10(1) allows the parties to determine the number of arbitrators. The statutory qualification is mandatory: the number so determined shall not be an even number.

sections.heading: 2. Statutory default of a sole arbitrator
sections.body: Where the parties have not determined the number of arbitrators, section 10(2) provides that the arbitral tribunal shall consist of a sole arbitrator.

sections.heading: 3. Reading the arbitration agreement
sections.body: The first question is whether the agreement actually determines tribunal size. If it does, apply section 10(1); if it does not, apply the section 10(2) default. Do not infer a three-member tribunal merely because that is common in some commercial clauses.

sections.heading: 4. Relationship with appointment provisions
sections.body: Section 10 addresses number, not the complete appointment procedure. Once the permissible composition is identified, the appointment provisions of the Act and the parties' agreed procedure must be considered.

examples.title: Three arbitrators
examples.body: The parties agree that their arbitral tribunal will comprise three arbitrators. Three is not an even number, so the determination satisfies section 10(1).

examples.title: Five arbitrators
examples.body: The parties expressly agree on five arbitrators. Five is not an even number, so the number is permissible under section 10(1), subject to the remaining statutory appointment framework.

examples.title: Even number specified
examples.body: The arbitration clause specifies four arbitrators. Section 10(1) expressly provides that the number determined by the parties shall not be even; the clause therefore cannot be treated as an unrestricted statutory choice of four.

examples.title: No number specified
examples.body: The arbitration agreement contains an arbitration clause but does not determine the number of arbitrators. Section 10(2) supplies the default of a sole arbitrator.

hypotheticals.question: The contract provides for three arbitrators. What does section 10 say about the number?
hypotheticals.analysis: Three is an odd number and therefore satisfies the express numerical condition in section 10(1). The appointment mechanism must then be considered under the applicable appointment provisions.

hypotheticals.question: The contract says nothing about the number of arbitrators. What is the statutory result?
hypotheticals.analysis: Section 10(2) provides that the arbitral tribunal shall consist of a sole arbitrator.

hypotheticals.question: The contract names four arbitrators. Can the clause be treated as a valid statutory determination simply because the parties agreed to it?
hypotheticals.analysis: No. Section 10(1) permits party determination only on the condition that the number shall not be an even number. The four-arbitrator stipulation therefore conflicts with the express numerical restriction.

hypotheticals.question: A party argues that every commercial arbitration should have three arbitrators. Is that the rule in section 10?
hypotheticals.analysis: No. Section 10 does not prescribe three as the universal number. It permits the parties to determine a non-even number and supplies a sole-arbitrator default where they have not determined the number.

rows.right: Parties have not determined the number.
Tribunal consists of a sole arbitrator.

distinctions.title: Number of arbitrators and appointment of arbitrators

rows.left: Permissible tribunal size and default size.
rows.right: How the arbitrator or arbitrators are appointed.
Determines the appointment procedure and statutory consequences of default or failure.

misconceptions.correction: It does not. Parties may determine a non-even number; absent determination, section 10(2) provides for a sole arbitrator.

misconceptions.trap: The parties can choose any number because arbitration is based on party autonomy.
misconceptions.correction: Party autonomy under section 10(1) is expressly limited by the prohibition on an even number.

misconceptions.trap: Section 10 itself sets out the full appointment procedure.
misconceptions.correction: Section 10 primarily regulates number. Appointment is dealt with by the succeeding statutory provisions and any validly agreed procedure.

questionsAndAnswers.question: What is the core rule under section 10?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: Section 10(1) permits the parties to determine the number of arbitrators, but the number cannot be even. If the parties do not determine the number, section 10(2) requires a sole arbitrator.
questionsAndAnswers.explanation: The provision combines party autonomy with an express numerical restriction and a statutory default.

questionsAndAnswers.question: How should counsel analyse tribunal size under section 10?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: First identify the contractual provision on tribunal size. Second determine whether the stated number is even or non-even. Third, if the parties did not determine the number, apply the sole-arbitrator default in section 10(2). Finally, address the separate appointment provisions rather than conflating composition with appointment procedure.
questionsAndAnswers.explanation: This keeps the analysis textually anchored to section 10 and its statutory neighbours.
